title: Webb unveils young stars across every stage of formation
caption: Part of the Orion Molecular Cloud OMC-2, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
celestial: constellation Orion · about 1280 light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, T. Megeath, M. Zamani (ESA/Webb) Acknowledgement: M. H. Özsaraç

recognition.text: Ranked #22 on ESA/Webb’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Layers of blue, green and yellowish gas and dust fill this scene, broken by thick clumps of cold dust so dark they block all light. Stars from small and orange to large and white or blue sit among the clouds, while streams of glowing whitish gas mark where jets from young stars strike their surroundings. This is a small northern part of OMC-2, 1280 light-years away, just behind and north of the Orion Nebula.
From stellar embryos to protoplanetary discs and newly formed stars, every stage of star birth appears within a patch just 2.5 light-years across.

The earliest stage is the protostar, a growing star fed with gas through a spinning disc. Infalling gas heats up and makes it glow, and the energy escapes as twin jets from its poles. In OMC-2 those jets drive shockwaves that heat the gas into sharp, glowing red ridges.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (6.69 x 3.93 arcminutes) and distance (1280 light years), the frame spans roughly 2.5 × 1.5 light-years. Its light set out about 1,300 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam maps shorter filters to blue and cyan and longer ones to green and red. The caption says blue and cyan hazes are scattered starlight, yellow to green is mostly PAH emission, orange, brown and some red mark warmer dust, and red ridges are outflow-heated gas.
understand.eye: All of this light is infrared, and in visible light the region's dust would hide the protostars completely.

explore: Visible light from OMC-2 is blocked by the dust around the Orion Nebula and by its own clouds, so only in infrared do the protostars start to shine through. By following the outflows, you can hunt for protostars still too buried to see directly.
The data come from a program studying star formation in OMC-2 and its neighbor OMC-3.
alt: Layers of blue, green and yellowish gas with dark clumps of dust, stars of varying size and color, and streams of glowing whitish gas from young stars' jets.
